items.title: Hide Tanaka interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 3, 2014
items.q: When you think about the great people, Cannonball Adderley and Miles Davis, and those fellas didn’t play together that long because they were destined to be their own leaders.

ctx.x: After eight years, I use like a karma. I don’t know why. Sometimes two musicians love the same kind of music and when they started they are both great musicians. But those two people never happen. Sometimes those things happen. But sometimes really great musicians, even if they play different kinds of music normally, but sometimes two musicians start to play, sometimes great things will happen. It’s kind of a mystery. It’s the same like general relationships too. Sports sometimes too. Those who start to play…

That is a great analogy. When you think about the great people, Cannonball Adderley and Miles Davis, and those fellas didn’t play together that long because they were destined to be their own leaders. And yesterday when we were talking to a couple of the students about bass solos, I think you had something interesting to say about bass solos. What do you feel about —

Yeah, the bass player — the most important thing is to play bass of course. But okay one of the reasons I really wanted to play bass is I really love the sound. But also at that time, the seventies, there were so many super bass players that came out. Stanley Clarke, Miroslav Vitous, Neils Henning, Jordan [inaudible], Eddie Gomez. So all those players became famous means they began to play in the up high register. So people understand what they’re playing. All the best players playing solos in the low register…
